claims.text: A high-entropy alloy in this hypothesis contains at least five elements, each at no less than 5 at.%.
The proposed starting material is a homogeneous, single-phase random solid solution dominated by Nb and Ta and containing a lower concentration of Ti.
Most previously studied type-A HEA superconductors contain large amounts of Nb and Ta and typically less than 20 at.% Ti.
Ti can be increased by replacing part of the Nb or Ta while retaining at least five elements at concentrations of 5 at.% or greater.
Increasing Ti relative to Nb and Ta changes the alloy's effective valence electron concentration.
Increasing Ti produces additional local lattice distortion through atomic-size mismatch.
Ti-induced lattice strain modifies the phonon spectrum.
Changes in valence electron concentration, lattice strain, and the phonon spectrum modify electron-phonon coupling strength.
Electron-phonon coupling governs the superconducting transition temperature in the proposed alloy.
Electron-phonon coupling governs the upper critical field in the proposed alloy.
Superconducting transition temperature in relevant HEA systems can evolve as a function of valence electron count.
Increasing Ti will produce a systematic shift in Tc relative to the Nb-Ta-rich baseline, potentially as an enhancement or a nonmonotonic variation.
An intermediate or increased Ti concentration may yield a higher upper critical field than the Nb-Ta-rich baseline.
The proposed Ti effect applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase disordered solid solution.
Phase separation, ordering, or intermetallic precipitation places a sample outside the hypothesis's applicability boundary.
The direction and magnitude of the Ti effect may depend on competition between enhanced electron-phonon coupling and increased scattering.
XRD and TEM can be used to verify phase purity and assess local lattice distortion in the composition series.
Tc and Hc2 can be compared across the Ti series using resistivity, magnetic susceptibility, and magnetotransport measurements under controlled low-temperature conditions.
The hypothesis is falsified if Ti is increased while the single-phase state is retained and neither Tc nor Hc2 changes systematically relative to the baseline.
